	string "VelaSight social cloud host override"
	default ""
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Hostname or IPv4 address of the social-session cloud, with no
		scheme and no port -- both of those are separate.

		Leave this empty for a normal build.  Empty no longer means
		"unconfigured": it means "use the factory default", which is
		CONFIG_VELASIGHT_PROVISION_CLOUD_HOST and is a real address.
		The Web provisioning record overrides both.

		Set it only to aim a whole build somewhere else -- a local mock
		during bring-up being the case it exists for, since a dotted quad
		here skips DNS and works before any resolver is configured.  A
		build that sets it is asking for that endpoint deliberately, so
		it wins over the factory default; it does not win over a
		provisioned record, because a device someone has actually
		provisioned should go where they said.

		If this and the factory default are both empty, the module is
		genuinely unconfigured: every operation fails with -ENODATA
		without opening a socket, and social mode refuses to start rather
		than timing out against a host that was never set.

config VS_SOCIAL_CLOUD_PORT
	int "VelaSight social cloud port override"
	default 18080
	range 1 65535
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Used only when VS_SOCIAL_CLOUD_HOST above is non-empty; the two
		travel together, because a port belongs to the host it was chosen
		for.  With the host left empty this value is ignored and
		CONFIG_VELASIGHT_PROVISION_CLOUD_PORT applies.

		The default is the port used throughout the cloud interface
		document's curl examples, which is the local-mock case this
		override targets.

config VS_SOCIAL_CLOUD_TLS
	bool "Reach the social cloud over TLS"
	default n
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Send /contest/v1/* over HTTPS through packages/ai_agent's
		vela_tls.c instead of cleartext HTTP.

		Off by default because the cloud is not there yet: the interface
		document specifies cleartext for the device-facing endpoints and
		its examples are plain HTTP, and no certificate chain has been
		captured for a real host.

		Understand what turning this on currently does and does not buy.
		vela_tls.c negotiates with MBEDTLS_SSL_VERIFY_OPTIONAL and this
		board has no CA bundle and no trusted time -- it forces the clock
		to a fixed 2026 value when it finds the year unset -- so the
		result is encryption without authentication.  That is strictly
		better than cleartext against a passive observer and no defence
		at all against an active one.  Do not describe a build with this
		enabled as having verified certificates until SNTP, a CA bundle
		and VERIFY_REQUIRED are all in place; see
		docs/plans/BK7258_OPENVELA_MIMO_NETWORK_PORTING_PLAN.md for the
		order those have to land in.

		This setting is independent of the presigned upload URL, whose
		scheme comes from the cloud's own response.

config VS_SOCIAL_DEVICE_ID
	string "VelaSight social cloud device id override"
	default ""
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Normally left empty.  The identifier is derived from the wlan0
		MAC address, which is unique and survives reboots without
		needing to be stored anywhere.

		This is the fallback for a board whose MAC cannot be read, and an
		escape hatch for cloud-side testing that wants a fixed, readable
		name.  Only letters, digits, '-', '_' and '.' are accepted;
		anything else is rejected at startup with a log line.

config VS_SOCIAL_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPE
	bool "Send Content-Type when transferring to the presigned URL"
	default n
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Whether the PUT that carries the JPEG or Ogg bytes to the
		presigned URL declares image/jpeg or audio/ogg.

		This exists as an option because object stores compute the
		presigned signature over a specific set of headers, and
		Content-Type is sometimes one of them: if it was signed, omitting
		it is rejected, and if it was not, sending it is rejected.  Both
		failures come back as HTTP 403 with an XML body.

		Default is off, because for this contest it is no longer an open
		question.  The cloud interface document's FDS upload example
		(section 7, storage) requires the header to be absent, spelling
		it as an explicit curl argument:

		  curl -i -X PUT '<presigned URL>' -H 'Content-Type:' \
		    --data-binary @/home/mi/a.jpg

		The empty -H 'Content-Type:' form is how curl suppresses a header
		it would otherwise supply, so FDS signs without it.  Sending one
		was measured (2026-08-31) as "Galaxy FDS Error: Signature Does
		Not Match" on every transfer while session open and upload
		registration both succeeded, which is the exact split this option
		was written to resolve.

		Turn it back on only for an object store known to sign the
		header; vs_cloud.c names this option in the 403 log line so the
		reverse case is equally traceable.

config VS_SOCIAL_REG_RESP_BYTES
	int "VelaSight social cloud registration response buffer (bytes)"
	default 4096
	range 1024 32768
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Buffer for the small responses: session open, upload
		registration, session close, and the object store's reply to a
		transfer.  The largest thing that lands here is a presigned URL,
		or an object store's XML error document.

		Sized separately from the result buffer below because one of
		these is allocated for every frame and every audio chunk, and
		sizing them all for a full session's timelines would waste PSRAM
		several times a second.

config VS_SOCIAL_RESP_MAX_BYTES
	int "VelaSight social cloud result response buffer (bytes)"
	default 65536
	range 8192 262144
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Buffer for getResult.  The end-of-session response is the large
		one: it carries the text minutes plus a full emotion timeline and
		a full audio timeline, one entry per sampled frame and per
		recognised sentence, so it grows with session length.

		A session whose minutes exceed this is reported as -E2BIG rather
		than truncated, because a clipped JSON record would be persisted"}

	int "VelaSight social cloud send/receive timeout (ms)"
	default 8000
	range 1000 60000
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---

# Session orchestration (app/velasight/vs_social.c).
#
# The schedule, not the protocol: how often to sample, how much to keep when
# the network stalls, and how sure the cloud has to be before an emotion is
# worth interrupting the user for.

config VS_SOCIAL_IMAGE_INTERVAL_MS
	int "VelaSight social image sampling interval (ms)"
	default 500
	range 200 2000
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		Target gap between captured frames.  The cloud interface document
		asks for 200 ms.

		What limits this is no longer the camera.  Earlier values here
		were sized against "252 ms per delivered frame", read from
		stop_capture's validator average, and that number was wrong in
		kind: it came from clock_systime_ticks() around work that ran at
		a contended priority, so it measured wall time including
		preemption rather than cost.  CONFIG_USEC_PER_TICK is 1000, too
		coarse to see the real figure at all.  With the DWT cycle counter
		(CONFIG_ARCH_PERF_EVENTS) a whole-frame entropy walk measures
		about 35 ms, and CONFIG_BK7258_CAMERA_JPEG_VALIDATE_MCUS brings
		that to 1-4 ms by settling alignment on a 128-macroblock prefix.
		The driver now delivers 17.39-17.87 fps at 480x480.

		The limit moved to the cloud round trip.  Each image is two of
		them -- register for a msgId and presigned URL, then PUT the
		bytes -- and one measured about 135 ms on a pooled connection.
		At 2 fps that is roughly 540 ms of round-trip time per second of
		session, which one worker can carry.  5 fps would need about
		1350 ms per second, so the document's rate needs the upload path
		to overlap requests before it means anything.

		Overshooting is no longer dangerous, only wasteful: the social
		workers run at VS_PRIORITY_SOCIAL, below the UI, so a backlog
		costs dropped frames rather than a frozen screen.  And the cloud
		stamps every emotionTimeline entry with its own timestamp, making
		no assumption about spacing, so a sparser timeline is a smaller
		timeline and not a broken one.

		Keep this equal to 1000 / VS_SOCIAL_CAPTURE_FPS.  The two knobs
		gate different stages and a mismatch wastes whole frames of
		validation on frames this application never reads -- see that
		option's help text.

		Keep this equal to 1000 / VS_SOCIAL_CAPTURE_FPS.  The two knobs"}

{"content":"config VS_SOCIAL_POLL_INTERVAL_MS
	int "VelaSight social result poll interval (ms)"
	default 1500
	range 500 5000
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		How often the session asks about the messages it has in flight.

		Independent of the sampling rate on purpose.  One getResult can
		carry many msgIds, so polling does not have to keep pace with
		uploading, and a shorter interval mostly buys extra round trips
		on a link that is already carrying the uploads.

config VS_SOCIAL_FINALIZE_TIMEOUT_MS
	int "VelaSight social finalize timeout (ms)"
	default 90000
	range 5000 180000
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		How long to poll for the minutes after asking the cloud to close
		the session.

		The close is asynchronous by design: the cloud answers with a
		msgId and status 40, and the minutes -- text summary, TTS URL and
		both timelines -- have to be polled for.  Generous by default
		because that work grows with the length of the conversation, and
		the alternative to waiting is showing the user a session that
		produced nothing.

		This was 30000, which measurement showed was not generous at all.
		Two runs against the staging cloud: 19.8 s on 2026-09-03 (from the
		AI端 server log) and 24.4 s on 2026-09-04 (measured end to end
		from the DELETE).  Both are the same trivial session -- a handful
		of frames, no faces found, so the summary was one sentence -- and
		they differ by nearly five seconds.  A real conversation has more
		to summarise and a voice to synthesise, and the jitter was already
		inside the old 5.6 s of headroom.

		Then 60000, chosen against that spread rather than its maximum,
		which three more measurements showed was still too tight:
		24.5 s, 44.3 s and 57.4 s on 2026-09-07.  The last one left 2.6 s
		of a 60 s budget, so the next slightly slower cloud would have
		shown the user a retry prompt for a session that was about to
		succeed.

		90000 is against the observed spread again, with the spread now
		known to reach nearly a minute.  Waiting costs a spinner; timing
		out early discards minutes the cloud did produce and asks the user
		to do something about a problem that does not exist.

config VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_BLOCK_BYTES
	int "VelaSight download write block (bytes)"
	default 32768
	range 512 262144
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---"}

{"content":"config VS_SOCIAL_UPLOAD_WORKERS
	int "VelaSight social upload workers"
	default 2
	range 1 2
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		How many threads pop the upload rings.  Each costs
		VS_SOCIAL_STACKSIZE_UPLOAD.

		More than one because an upload is two serial round trips to two
		different hosts -- register with the business server, then PUT the
		bytes to the presigned URL -- and one worker can only be inside one
		of them at a time.  Measured 2026-09-07: 984 ms per item, against a
		budget of two pooled round trips at about 135 ms each.

		The cost is also very nearly independent of payload size, which is
		what says the limit is latency rather than bandwidth: in one
		session an image-heavy report window averaged 869 ms per item while
		an audio-heavy one, carrying a quarter of the bytes, averaged
		1636 ms.  Bandwidth would have made the small items faster.
		Latency does not care, and latency is what overlapping requests
		hides.

		The two registrations still take turns, because they share one
		cleartext connection that vs_cloud.c serializes -- deliberately, so
		that the connection which opened the session stays the one every
		request uses.  What overlaps is one item's registration against
		another item's transfer.

		Two is the ceiling, and it is set outside this application.
		vela_tls.c pools connections in CONN_POOL_SIZE slots, two by
		default, and reads every response through one of TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT
		static 8 KB buffers, also two.  A third concurrent transfer would
		find no pool slot and open an unpooled connection -- a full
		handshake per upload -- and would block waiting for a response
		buffer.  Raising it here without raising those would be slower, not
		faster.

		Set to 1 to get the old single-worker behaviour.  A session still
		runs if only some workers start: the rest are throughput, and only
		failing to start any is fatal.

config VS_SOCIAL_STACKSIZE_CAPTURE
	int "VelaSight social capture-thread stack size"
	default 8192
	range 4096 65536
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		The shallowest of the four: a poll, an ioctl and a copy, with a
		measured frame of 24 bytes.  Left at the old shared default because
		there is no reason to trim it, and against a frame that shallow the
		whole value is headroom.
"}

/* ── LLM Watchdog ──────────────────────────────────────────── */
/* Agent-level timeout for a single LLM call (seconds).
 * If llm_chat_tools takes longer than this, the agent treats it as
 * a timeout and replies with a user-friendly error message.
 * The socket-level SO_RCVTIMEO (AGENT_LLM_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_SEC)
 * acts as the hard backstop that actually unblocks the read. */
#ifndef AGENT_LLM_TIMEOUT_SEC
#define AGENT_LLM_TIMEOUT_SEC 60
#endif

/* Socket-level read timeout applied via SO_RCVTIMEO in vela_tls.
 * Must be >= AGENT_LLM_TIMEOUT_SEC to allow the agent-level
 * watchdog to fire first on normal slow responses.  Set higher
 * to cover TLS handshake + full response read. */
#define AGENT_LLM_SOCKET_TIMEOUT_SEC 120

/* ── Timezone (POSIX TZ format) ────────────────────────────── */
#define AGENT_TIMEZONE "CST-8"

/* ── LLM ────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
#define AGENT_LLM_DEFAULT_MODEL ""
/* Overridable, and deliberately far below the provider's ceiling.
 *
 * On a spoken path this number is a latency budget, not a capacity: it bounds
 * how long the model may keep generating before it has to stop, and a reply
 * the user waits through is worth less the longer it is.  Measured on
 * hardware, one 319-byte answer took 95 s to generate at the old 4096.  The
 * voice prompt already asks for at most 150 Chinese characters, which needs a
 * few hundred tokens, so this leaves generous room while cutting the worst
 * case by a factor of four.
 */

#ifndef AGENT_LLM_MAX_TOKENS
#define AGENT_LLM_MAX_TOKENS 1024
#endif
/* Applies to the OpenAI-compatible hosts, which is the path MiMo uses.
 *
 * With deep thinking disabled this budget is the answer alone rather than
 * thinking plus answer, so a spoken reply needs a small fraction of the old
 * 16384.  It stays well above what the voice prompt asks for -- at most 150
 * Chinese characters -- so a provider that ignores the thinking switch still
 * produces a complete reply rather than a truncated one.
 */

#ifndef AGENT_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_OPENAI
#define AGENT_LLM_MAX_TOKENS_OPENAI 2048
#endif
#define AGENT_LLM_API_HOST ""
#define AGENT_LLM_API_PATH "/v1/chat/completions"
#ifndef AGENT_LLM_API_URL
#define AGENT_LLM_API_URL ""
#endif
#define AGENT_LLM_API_VERSION "openai"
#define AGENT_LLM_MAX_RETRIES 3
#define AGENT_LLM_RETRY_BASE_SEC 2
#define AGENT_LLM_STREAM_BUF_SIZE (8 * 1024)
#define AGENT_LLM_MAX_RESP_SIZE \
    (512 * 1024) /* hard cap for growable resp buffer */

/* ── Qwen (Alibaba DashScope) backend constants ─────────────── */
#define AGENT_LLM_QWEN_HOST "dashscope.aliyuncs.com"
#define AGENT_LLM_QWEN_PATH "/compatible-mode/v1/chat/completions"
#define AGENT_LLM_QWEN_MODEL "qwen-turbo"

/* ── OpenRouter (unified multi-model gateway) ───────────────── */"}

thinking:
I'm piecing together the performance breakdown: each item takes about 1050 milliseconds total, split between a registration call at 173ms and a put operation at 874ms. These are two separate round trips hitting different hosts over different transports—the registration goes as cleartext HTTP to the staging health endpoint while using a single persistent socket connection.

The put request goes over HTTPS to the API endpoint through a TLS connection pool with just 2 slots, and there's a fixed ~10ms drain penalty on every pooled TLS request from a blocking receive timeout that always expires when there's no data waiting. The cleartext exchanges are all serialized by a lock, and there's no TCP_NODELAY enabled anywhere, so headers and bodies get sent as separate writes. The TLS pool doesn't support session resumption either, so eviction means a full handshake. Each item also triggers multiple memory allocations and a JSON parse.

Now I'm thinking about what's actually modifiable—the app code is fair game, but the vela_tls transport layer lives in the external packages directory, though I did commit that overlay before so it might be changeable.

Let me map out which optimizations are in app/ versus external/, then break down where that 1050ms is actually going. The registration call alone takes 173ms per item—that's one cleartext round trip on a kept socket with a small request and response, so the wire time is negligible and most of that delay is lock contention, RTT, and server processing.

The put operation is more interesting: 12895 bytes taking 874ms. At the measured download speed of 42 KB/s (336 kbit/s), symmetric upload would predict around 307ms just for bandwidth, but we're seeing 874ms—that's 570ms unaccounted for. Some of that is the guaranteed 10ms drain per request, and the rest is likely TLS record encryption overhead. On a 480 MHz Cortex-M33 without hardware crypto acceleration, encrypting 12.9 KB with mbedtls AES-256-GCM in software is going to be expensive.

Let me work through the crypto cost: at roughly 100 cycles per byte for AES-256-GCM, that's about 1.29 million cycles, which translates to around 2.7ms at 480 MHz—not huge even at the pessimistic end of 500 cycles/byte (13ms). The real culprit is probably Nagle's algorithm interacting with how the data gets split across multiple writes. The header record is small (200-300 bytes of ciphertext), and without TCP_NODELAY, Nagle will hold it waiting for acknowledgment before sending the body record.

Since the body is about 12.9 KB (roughly 9 MSS), the first 8 full segments transmit but the final partial segment stalls until the header is ACKed—adding roughly one RTT to the latency. So the total overhead is around 307 bytes of wire time plus 10ms drain time plus that RTT delay from Nagle, plus whatever FDS processing the server adds on the response side.

Now looking at the throughput constraints: registration is the global bottleneck at 173ms per item, capping throughput at 5.78 items/s, while the PUT operation with 2 pool slots maxes out at 2.29 items/s. With 2 workers each cycling through registration and PUT serially, the theoretical ceiling is 1.90 items/s, but we're only observing 1.29 items/s—the gap suggests the workers aren't fully saturated because the image queue is limited to 2 slots and the sampler itself is rate-constrained.

At the current 750ms interval, the system is actually near capacity: images arrive at 1.33/s plus audio at 0.5/s equals 1.83 items/s offered, which nearly matches our 1.90 items/s capacity. To improve throughput, I need to either reduce the per-item cost or increase parallelism.

The biggest structural win would be to prefetch registration: since the register call only produces a msgId and presignedUrl and doesn't depend on the image bytes themselves, I can decouple it from the critical path by maintaining a small pool of pre-registered tickets ready to use immediately when a frame arrives.

This would cut per-item cost from the serial register+put (1050ms) down to just the put operation (874ms)—a 17% reduction. The challenge is that the register body includes a timestamp (when the media was produced) and msgEvent (image vs audio), so each prefetched ticket is bound to a type and carries a timestamp that predates the actual frame. I can handle msgEvent by maintaining separate pools for images and audio, but the timestamp is problematic—I need to verify whether the cloud actually uses it for the emotionTimeline or if it's just echoed back.

Looking at the data, emotionTimeline had 82 unique timestamps matching exactly 82 uploaded images, so the cloud almost certainly echoes the device's registration timestamp into the timeline. If I prefetch tickets, frames would get stamped with the ticket's creation time rather than the actual shutter time. With a pool of 2 tickets and 750ms intervals, that's up to 1.5 seconds of skew. The cloud's timeline is already unsorted with backward gaps up to 6 seconds, so 1.5 seconds would technically be within existing noise—but it's still a correctness issue I'd be deliberately introducing.

Keeping prefetch depth at exactly 1 means the ticket gets minted while the previous item is being uploaded, so it's still ~874ms early. This feels like a tradeoff worth surfacing rather than hiding: it's the biggest performance win available in the app layer, but it costs timestamp accuracy by one item interval. The core constraint is that the register request requires a timestamp, so there's no way around committing one when minting the ticket. The real option is overlapping the registration of the next item with the upload of the current one within the same worker—true pipelining without getting ahead of capture.

The cleanest approach is restructuring the worker as a two-stage pipeline: the first stage pops from the ring, registers the item, and pushes the result (item, message ID, presigned URL) to an intermediate queue; the second stage pops from that queue and uploads. This way registration uses the actual produced timestamp of a real item with no error, the two stages overlap across items, registration stays serialized at 173ms giving 5.78 items/s capacity, and uploads have 2 pool slots at 874ms giving 2.29 items/s capacity.

The system bottleneck becomes 2.29 items/s (a 20% improvement over today's 1.90) with no correctness issues and the same 2 TLS pool slots. The tradeoff is one extra thread (3 total instead of 2) and a slightly larger stack, but the intermediate queue just holds already-allocated buffers. However, this does increase PSRAM pressure since item buffers now sit in the intermediate queue while the previous item is uploading, rather than being freed immediately after each PUT.

Now I'm weighing whether that 20% gain justifies the added complexity. Let me also look at other potential improvements, like removing the 10 ms pooled-connection drain in the TLS request handler.

Every pooled reuse does a blocking read with a 10 ms timeout, which means it always waits the full 10 ms even when there's nothing to drain—that's 1.64 seconds of pure sleep per session across 164 items, sitting right on the critical path of every PUT. I could fix this with non-blocking I/O or a zero-timeout poll check to see if there's actually data before reading. It's only about 1% of the total cycle time, but it's a guaranteed win with zero risk, and it also helps the TTS download path.

The bigger issue is TCP_NODELAY on the cleartext path. The register writes a ~300-byte header and ~200-byte body as two separate sends, which triggers Nagle's algorithm—the second small write waits for the ACK of the first. On a ~100 ms RTT link, that's an extra 100 ms on every register, which could account for most of the 173 ms bottleneck. I can fix this either by setting TCP_NODELAY on the socket during connection setup, or better yet, coalesce both writes into a single send call since the header buffer is already allocated in PSRAM. I need to be precise about the RTT claim—without direct measurement, I can't pin down the exact magnitude, but the structural issue (two small writes without NODELAY) is definitely a known latency pattern, so I should frame it as a cheap optimization to validate empirically. Now looking at batching the getResult poll: it runs every 1500 ms on the same serialized socket and can return up to 64 KB, which blocks both workers while holding the lock.

The register latency variance I'm seeing—ranging from 69 to 303 ms—appears to correlate directly with poll collisions. At 1.29 items/s with a 1.5 s poll interval, roughly every other register hits the queue behind a poll, and if that poll takes ~300 ms with a large response body, it injects that delay into the register times. The low values (69/70/70 ms) are likely registers that avoided the poll entirely, while the high ones (240/267/303 ms) collided with it—that 69-to-303 spread is the smoking gun.

I'm weighing the tradeoffs: lengthening the poll interval reduces collisions but slows feedback for the debounce window; giving the poll its own connection breaks the single-socket invariant that routes to the right cloud instance; making the poll conditional on having data to fetch might already be happening; or reducing the poll's response payload could be the quickest win.

The simpler approach is to make the poll adaptive—skip the round trip when nothing's in flight, and when items are pending, align the poll timing to not interfere with register operations. Since the register is on the critical path and the poll isn't, prioritizing the register's latency makes sense.

I could use a non-blocking lock attempt for the poll; if a register holds the lock, skip that cycle. Missing a poll costs about 1.5 seconds of latency, while blocking a register costs 200 ms per item per cycle—an easy trade-off. But I need to guard against the poll starving; I'd cap consecutive skips at 2 before forcing a lock acquisition.

Now looking at the TLS connection pool—raising `CONN_POOL_SIZE` and `TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT` from 2 to 3 or 4 would allow more concurrent uploads, which matters given the 874 ms put latency.

However, each extra slot adds 20–30 KB for an mbedtls context, and each raw buffer is 8 KB static. On a 344 KB RAM budget, that's significant. Plus, `CONN_POOL_SIZE` is a Kconfig symbol, so I need to figure out whether it's defined in external/ or board/—if it's in a Kconfig somewhere, I could set it via defconfig in board/, though that's not ideal since board/ isn't part of the app.

But here's the catch: `TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT` is capped at 2 regardless of `CONN_POOL_SIZE`, so adding more connections without raising the buffer count doesn't help—a third concurrent PUT would still block waiting for a buffer. Raising the pool alone buys nothing, exactly as the Kconfig help warns. So option E needs two external/ changes and costs ~30 KB more RAM, making it lower priority.

Now looking at option F: reducing bytes, where audio turns out to be the expensive item per byte.

The measurements show an audio-heavy report window averaged 1636 ms despite carrying a quarter of the bytes compared to an image-heavy window at 869 ms. Audio chunks are only 6 KB each (2 seconds of 16 kHz Opus at 24000 bps) versus 12.9 KB for images, so they're half the size but cost more—pure latency again. Audio makes up 61 of 164 items (37% of uploads) but only 22% of the bytes, so each audio chunk carries disproportionate cost.

I'm considering lengthening audio chunks from 2000 ms to 4000 ms, which would cut audio items in half (61 → 31) and free up roughly 31 seconds of worker time in a 127-second session—about 25% of one worker's capacity that could go to images. But the spec says devices send images every 200 ms and audio every 2 seconds, and the cloud's ASR might expect ~2-second segments. Since `audioTimeline` has been empty for 6 sessions, the audio uploads are currently producing zero value anyway.

The real fix is to make audio work properly, but adjusting `CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_AUDIO_CHUNK_MS` from 2000 to 3000 or 4000 is a straightforward app-level config change with clear throughput benefits—worth presenting as an option with the tradeoff clearly named.

Presigned URLs can't be reused since each one maps to a single object, so skipping register for retries won't work. I'm also looking at image compression options—there's already a `CONFIG_BK7258_JPEG_BITRATE_PCT` setting in the board config that can lower bitrate.

Lowering it to 60% would produce frames around 8 KB, but since uploads are latency-dominated rather than bandwidth-dominated, halving the bytes again only gains maybe 15% faster uploads. The image quality hit could matter for the emotion model, so this has low leverage and isn't an app-level change anyway.

The bigger opportunity is that 16 out of 103 frames failed because there was no usable face detected—that's 15.5% wasted work. If the device could pre-screen for faces locally, it would save 16 round-trip pairs and about 16.8 seconds of worker time. The problem is there's no local face detector available in velasight; the face detection code lives in a separate camera preview app.

There's a `preview_face.c` file in the app directory that might be worth investigating as a potential gate for uploads, though it's speculative and could introduce a new failure mode if it drops frames the cloud would have classified. Low priority to pursue.

Increasing the image queue from 2 slots to 4 would absorb timing jitter and let the sampler run more frequently without dropping frames when both workers are busy. That's an extra 52 KB of memory for the queue buffers.

The tradeoff is that a deeper queue delays older frames, which means emotion results arrive later. My adaptive floor uses overflow to measure capacity, so a deeper queue would let it probe faster. Since I'm now tracking timestamps correctly through the pipeline, the frame age stays accurate even if it's uploaded later — the cost is just result latency, not correctness. This is probably the second-best lever after the pipeline itself: bump the queue to 4 slots and let the sampler settle at a shorter interval.

A deeper queue doesn't actually increase throughput, but it does improve utilization. Right now at 1.83 offered versus 1.90 capacity, workers are nearly saturated, so the queue mainly prevents drops rather than raising throughput. It lets the sampler push the interval down without dropping frames, which increases the image rate until workers hit their ceiling. So it helps reach that 1.90 limit with fewer drops.

Now I'm ranking the options by expected gain divided by risk and effort, starting with app-only changes. Coalescing the header and body into a single write for the cleartext register is a small change with no behavior impact — it removes a Nagle round trip from every registration and I'd add TCP_NODELAY too.  Expected improvement is around 90–120 ms, which is 5–8% of the item cost with zero risk.

Letting the register win the lock over the poll is another small change that could collapse the register variance down toward the 69–70 ms floor, since the poll is currently injecting 150–230 ms into registrations. That's another 5–8% gain.

A two-stage pipeline with one registrar and two transferrers would be a moderate restructure that makes capacity put-bound, jumping from 1.90 to 2.29 items per second — a 20% boost — without compromising timestamps. It costs one thread stack and a couple of extra buffers in flight.

Bumping the image queue slots from 2 to 4 converts drops into delay and lets the sampler reach true capacity with low risk. Extending the audio chunk window from 2000 to 3000 or 4000 milliseconds frees up 25–33% of the upload work currently producing an empty audioTimeline, though that needs the user's input and ideally we'd first understand why audioTimeline is empty.

Removing the 10 millisecond drain frees about 1% and helps TLS download performance too. Raising the connection pool size and TLS raw buffer count to 3–4 would help with throughput on the external side.

Prefetching registration tickets is the single biggest win since it removes registration from the item path entirely, but it sacrifices timestamp accuracy — I should present it as an option and recommend against it unless the cloud confirms registration timestamps aren't used for emotionTimeline.

Looking at the combined performance picture: today we're at 1050 ms per item with 2 workers and 1.90 items/s capacity, observing 1.29. With the registration and pipeline fixes, we'd drop to 967 ms per item and hit 2.07 items/s, and the pipeline becomes put-bound at 874 milliseconds.

Adding the prefetch brings us to 2.29 items/s in the app layer alone, a 21% gain. If we also allow the external pool raises with 4 slots and 4 buffers, we could theoretically reach 4.63 items/s — a 140% improvement — though at that point the sampler and queue become the limiting factors instead.

The core constraint is that 2 TLS pool slots times 874 ms creates a hard ceiling around 2.3 items/s for app-only changes. Hitting the document's target of 5 fps requires expanding the pool, which falls outside the app layer. The put operation itself takes 874 ms for 12.9 KB, split across wire time at the observed 42 KB/s download rate, a 10 ms drain, Nagle effects, and FDS processing — but without instrumentation I can't pinpoint whether the upload link is the actual bottleneck.

To properly diagnose this, I'd need to instrument the put operation to measure write time, first-response-byte latency, and full-response time separately, though that instrumentation would live in the external layer through `vela_tls`. I could time around the `vela_https_request` call since that's already tracked as `transfer_ms`, but splitting it further requires external layer changes. I'm exploring whether there's an app-only experiment that could isolate wire latency from server latency, though the options I'm considering either require board-level changes or don't actually help.

Actually, I can do this cleanly within the app: compare put times for audio (6 KB) versus image (12.9 KB) items. The report already mixes them, but I could add per-type accumulators. If put times are similar regardless of size, it's pure latency; if they scale with bytes, it's wire-bound. This is a cheap diagnostic that directly tells me whether parallelism or byte-reduction is the right optimization lever. The Kconfig help already hints at the answer—audio-heavy windows were slower—but I haven't cleanly measured this per-half. I should recommend this measurement first since it's good engineering discipline: the biggest proposed change needs to be justified by cleanly measuring latency-boundedness.

I'll organize the response as budget → where time provably goes → options ranked → what to measure first. Keep it focused and read-only, no edits. I should also note that it's worth verifying whether `social_poll_once` skips when nothing is in flight, since that affects option 2, but I have enough to write the response now.

读了完整链路（vs_social.c 上传 worker、vs_cloud.c 两段往返、vela_tls.c 连接池）。先把 1050 ms 拆开。

## 每项 1050 ms 花在哪

一次上传是**两段串行往返，打到两个不同主机、走两套不同传输**：

| | reg | put |
|---|---|---|
| 端点 | `[REDACTED-INTERNAL-URL] | `staging-cnbj2-fds.api.xiaomi.net:443` |
| 传输 | 明文 HTTP（`VS_SOCIAL_CLOUD_TLS=n`） | vela_tls 连接池 |
| 并发 | **1**（单 socket + `g_cloud_keep_lock`） | 2（`CONN_POOL_SIZE=2`） |
| 实测 | 173 ms | 874 ms |

容量算式：每个 worker 串行跑 reg→put = 1050 ms，2 worker → **1.90 项/s**。实测 1.29，而采样环收敛后供给是 1.33 图/s + 0.48 音频/s = 1.81 项/s —— 基本贴着容量在跑，系统已经饱和。

put 874 ms 搬 12895 字节 = **14.4 KB/s**，而同一条链路下载 TTS 跑到 42 KB/s。按 42 KB/s 算线路时间只需 307 ms，剩下 ~560 ms 是往返、FDS 处理和固定开销。**这条路是延迟受限，不是带宽受限**——上游把图片压小 26% 只换来 put 快 22%，正是这个结论的直接证据。

## 三个可证的固定开销

**1. 明文 register 是 Nagle 的教科书案例。** `cloud_plain_http_once()` 把 header 和 body 分两次 `send()`（vs_cloud.c:1297-1312），全仓库没有任何地方设 `TCP_NODELAY`（只有 `app/web_tool` 和 `app/netbench` 有）。register 的 body 只有 224 字节（`char body[224]`），header 约 300 字节 —— 两个小写入背靠背，第二个要等第一个的 ACK。

**2. poll 在抢 register 的锁。** `g_cloud_keep_lock` 序列化的不只是两个 worker 的 register，还有每 1500 ms 一次的 getResult，而 getResult 的响应缓冲是 65536 字节。看这次 16 个窗口的 reg 值：

```
218 154 178 70 173 120 303 221 214 267 130 240 69 165 70 177
```

`69/70/70` 和 `240/267/303` 差了 4 倍。69 ms 应该是没撞上 poll 的裸往返，230+ 的是排在 poll 后面的。**poll 大约往 register 里注入了 150–230 ms**，而 register 在每一项的关键路径上，poll 不在。

**3. 每次复用池化 TLS 连接固定付 10 ms。** vela_tls.c:944-967 在复用前做排空读，socket 是阻塞模式（`mbedtls_net_set_block`）+ `SO_RCVTIMEO=10ms`，没有待读数据时**必然等满 10 ms**。164 项 = 1.64 s 纯睡眠，而且 TTS 下载也在付。

另外每项还有：4 对 PSRAM alloc/free、一次 `malloc(4096)`、一次 `cJSON_Parse`、无 TLS 会话复用（池位被驱逐就是完整握手）。

## 方案，按 收益/风险 排

### 只改 app/

**① 合并 register 的 header 和 body 成一次 send + 设 TCP_NODELAY**（约 10 行）

header 缓冲已经是 `CLOUD_PATH_MAX + 512` ≈ 3.4 KB 的 PSRAM 分配，224 字节的 body 直接追加进去做单次 `cloud_send_all()` 就行，连 socket 选项都不用碰。`TCP_NODELAY` 在 `cloud_connect()` 加一行作为兜底。

预期 reg 173 → 90–120 ms，约占整项成本 5–8%。零风险，PUT 走 TLS 不受影响。

**② 让 register 优先于 poll 拿锁**（小改）

poll 用 `pthread_mutex_trylock`，拿不到就跳过本轮，带一个连续跳过上限（比如 2 次）防饿死。少一轮 poll 的代价是 1.5 s 的结果延迟；堵住一次 register 的代价是每个 poll 周期给 2 项各加 200 ms。这个交换很划算。预期 reg 收敛到 70–90 ms 那一档。

**③ 改成两级流水：1 个 registrar + 2 个 transferrer**（中等重构，收益最大）

现在一个 worker 串行做完 reg 和 put。改成 registrar 从环里取件、register 完把 `(item, msgId, presignedUrl)` 推到中间队列，transferrer 从中间队列取件做 PUT。

- 容量从 min 变成 put 受限：`874 ms / 2 池位` = **2.29 项/s**（今天 1.90），**+20%**
- registrar 侧 173 ms 串行 = 5.78 项/s，配①②后到 11 项/s，绰绰有余
- **不牺牲时间戳精度**：register 的是真实在队的 item，`produced_ms` 照旧准确

代价：多一个 16 KB 栈，中间队列多压 2 个 buffer（约 26 KB PSRAM）。

**④ `IMAGE_QUEUE_SLOTS` 2 → 4**（Kconfig 一行，`social_queue_flush()` 的数组已按常量定尺）

2 个槽意味着两个 worker 一忙采样器立刻溢出。加到 4 把"丢帧"变成"延迟"——而 `produced_ms` 现在是正确携带的，所以延迟上传不影响时间戳。让自适应底线能探到真实容量而不是被队列深度限死。

**⑤ `AUDIO_CHUNK_MS` 2000 → 3000/4000**（Kconfig，需要你定）

61 个音频块占了 164 项里的 37%，只贡献 22% 的字节。而 `audioTimeline` 已经连续 6 次会话为空 —— **这 37% 的上传工作目前产出为零**。翻倍块长能释放约 30 项 × 1050 ms = 31 s 的 worker 时间，等于一个 worker 25% 的容量，直接换成图片吞吐。

代价：偏离文档的"2s 发送一次音频"，而且云端 ASR 可能对分段长度有预期。我倾向**先修音频为什么是空的，而不是先节流它**——这是拿一个坏了的功能换吞吐，方向不对。

### 需要改 external/

**⑥ 干掉那 10 ms 排空等待**（vela_tls.c，几行）

用 `poll(fd, POLLIN, 0)` 先看有没有数据再读，没有就跳过。省 1% 并且 TTS 下载同样受益。零风险。

**⑦ `CONN_POOL_SIZE` 和 `TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT` 提到 4**

这是 app/ 天花板之外的唯一出路。注意**两个都要提**：`TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT (CONN_POOL_SIZE < 2 ? 1 : 2)` 硬编码上限 2，只提池位的话第三个并发 PUT 会在 `tls_raw_acquire()` 阻塞在 buffer 0 上，`Kconfig` 的 help 已经写明这点。

代价：每个额外池位一个 mbedtls context（约 20–30 KB），每个额外 raw buffer 8 KB 静态。344 KB RAM 里要挤出 ~30 KB。

配上③之后容量到 `874/4 = 4.58 项/s`。

## 累积估算

| 组合 | 容量 | 相对今天 |
|---|---|---|
| 今天 | 1.90 项/s | — |
| ①② | 2.07 项/s | +9% |
| ①②③ | 2.29 项/s | +21% |
| ①②③⑥ | 2.31 项/s | +22% |
| ①②③⑥⑦ | 4.63 项/s | **+144%** |

**只改 app/ 的天花板是 ~2.3 项/s**，因为「2 个 TLS 池位 × 874 ms」是一道硬墙，③把系统推到墙上之后①②再快也没用。文档要的 200 ms 图片间隔（5 图/s）必须动 external/ 才有可能。

## 建议先做一次测量

③和⑦都建立在"put 是延迟受限"这个判断上。这个判断有间接证据（图片小 26% 只快 22%；Kconfig help 记录的音频重窗口反而更慢），但没有干净的直接测量。

**最便宜的验证：把 put 按 item 类型分别累计。** 音频块 6 KB、图片 12.9 KB，字节数差一倍：

- 如果 `put(audio) ≈ put(image)` → 纯延迟，③⑦是对的杠杆，压缩字节没用
- 如果 `put` 随字节线性 → 带宽受限，该去动 `BK7258_JPEG_BITRATE_PCT` 而不是加并发

这是 app/ 内几行累加器的事，一次会话就能定性。在此之前我不想动③那样的重构。

要我先做这个测量（①②可以顺便一起，都是低风险），还是直接上①②③？⑤和⑦需要你先定：⑤是否接受偏离文档的音频间隔，⑦是否允许改 external/ 并且能接受 ~30 KB RAM。
完整评估可执行优化方案，只读

完整评估。先给结论：**上传吞吐有一道 2.29 项/s 的硬墙，位置在 vela_tls 的 2 个连接池位 × 874 ms 的 PUT，而且这道墙搬不动**（下面有 RAM 算术）。所以真正可执行的杠杆只有两类：把 reg 从关键路径上挪走，和减少总请求数。

## 已核实的约束

| 约束 | 值 | 出处 | 可改？ |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 连接池位 | `CONN_POOL_SIZE 2` | vela_tls.c:308-313 | external/ 托管覆盖层 |
| TLS 响应缓冲 | `TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT (POOL<2?1:2)` 硬上限 2 | vela_tls.c:656-661 | 同上 |
| `CONFIG_AI_AGENT_TLS_CONN_POOL_SIZE` | **全仓库没有 Kconfig 条目** | grep 无命中 | 只能改 `#else` 默认值 |
| 每连接 mbedtls 记录缓冲 | `IN=16384` + `OUT=16384` | 生成的 config.h | board/ defconfig |
| 明文 API 连接 | **单 socket**，`g_cloud_keep_lock` 全序列化 | vs_cloud.c:373, 1627 | app/ |
| 池化连接固定排空 | **10 ms 阻塞读**，无数据时必然等满 | vela_tls.c:944-967 | external/ |
| `TCP_NODELAY` | 两条路径都没设 | 全仓库只有 web_tool / netbench | app/（明文）+ external/（TLS） |
| header/body 分两次写 | 是，两条路径都是 | vs_cloud.c:1297-1312；vela_tls.c:610-650 | 同上 |
| `hdr_cap` | `CLOUD_PATH_MAX + 512` ≈ 4 KB；register body 224 B | vs_cloud.c:1206 | 合并空间充裕 |
| `IMAGE_QUEUE_SLOTS` | 2，range **1–8** | Kconfig:1404 | app/ |
| `AUDIO_CHUNK_MS` | 2000，range **500–5000** | Kconfig:881 | app/ |
| poll 空转 | 已有 `n == 0` 提前返回 | vs_social.c `social_poll_once` | 不用改 |
| external/ 覆盖层 | 17 文件 + 树摘要 `d498a0b5…`，`prepare.sh` 拒绝未知修改 | manifest.tsv, prepare.sh:563 | 改文件需重算摘要 |

`vela_tls.c` 和 `include/agent_config.h` **都在那 17 个托管文件里**，所以改它们是改已有文件、不动 `EXPECTED_MANAGED=58`，只需重算 manifest 树摘要——我之前那个 `feat(external): carry the vela_tls streaming sink` 提交走的就是这条路。

## 逐项评估

### ① 合并 register 的 header+body 成单次 send（+ TCP_NODELAY）

**机制。** register 是 ~300 B header + 224 B body 两次 `send()`。第二个小写入必须等第一个的 ACK——这是 Nagle 最典型的形态。`hdr_cap` ≈ 4 KB，body 224 B，追加进去做单次 `cloud_send_all()` 空间绰绰有余。

**改动面。** `cloud_plain_http_once()` 一处，带 `body_len <= hdr_cap - pos` 守卫。这个函数是通用的（还服务 getResult 无 body、session open/close 小 body、以及 TLS 关闭时的 PUT 大 body），守卫让大 body 自动回落到两次写。`cloud_connect()` 加一行 `TCP_NODELAY` 兜底。约 15 行。

**算术。** reg 的 16 个窗口最低值是 **69/70/70 ms**，那应该是没撞 poll 的裸路径。若 RTT ≈ 35 ms，69 ms ≈ 2 个 RTT（一个被 Nagle 吃掉，一个是响应）。合并后应降到约 1 个 RTT ≈ **35 ms**。

**风险。** 极低。可证伪的预测：reg 的最低窗口值从 69–70 掉到 30–40。

**判定：做。** 十几行换掉一个完整 RTT。

### ② 让 register 优先于 getResult 拿锁

**机制。** `g_cloud_keep_lock` 同时序列化两个 worker 的 register 和每 1500 ms 一次的 getResult（响应缓冲 65536 B）。register 在每一项的关键路径上，poll 不在。

**证据。** reg 的 16 个窗口值：`218 154 178 70 173 120 303 221 214 267 130 240 69 165 70 177`。最低 69、最高 303，差 4.4 倍。这个离散度只有"排队等 poll"能解释——**poll 大约注入 150–230 ms**。

**改动面。** poll 侧用 `pthread_mutex_trylock`，失败就跳过本轮，带连续跳过上限（2 次后必须正常拿锁，防饿死）。需要给 `cloud_api_call` 加一个"try"变体或一个可选标志，约 30 行。

**算术。** 少一轮 poll 的代价是 1.5 s 结果延迟（`ALERT_WINDOW_MS=20000`、`ADVICE_TIMEOUT_MS=30000` 都远大于此，无影响）。堵一次 register 的代价是每个 poll 周期给约 2 项各加 200 ms。reg 均值应从 173 收敛到 80–90。

**风险。** 低。饿死上限是唯一需要小心的地方。

**判定：做。**

### ③ 两级流水：1 registrar + 2 transferrer

**机制。** 现在每个 worker 串行跑 reg(173)+put(874)=1050 ms，2 worker = 1.90 项/s。拆开后 transferrer 的周期只有 put = 874 ms，2 个 = **2.29 项/s**。registrar 串行 173 ms = 5.78 项/s，不是瓶颈。

注意今天 reg 和 put **已经跨 worker 重叠了**（锁只序列化 reg-vs-reg），1.90 这个数已经包含了这层重叠。③的收益来自把 reg 从每个 worker 的串行周期里彻底移出。

**改动面。** 中等重构：
- 新增中间队列（`(slot, msg_id, presigned)`，深度 2–3）
- `social_upload_worker` 拆成 `social_register_worker` 和 `social_transfer_worker`
- `vs_cloud_social_upload()` 拆成 `_register()` 和 `_transfer()` 两个导出函数（vs_cloud.h 变化）
- 计数器归属：`inflight_add` 该在 register 后还是 transfer 后？必须是 **register 后**（msgId 那时才有，而且 PUT 失败的 msgId 云端也会返回 status 30）
- 采样环的 AIMD 恢复必须留在 transfer 侧（"图片真的送出去了"才是链路有余量的证据）
- teardown 顺序：`producers_done` → registrar 退出 → 中间队列排空 → transferrer 退出 → 然后才是 `cloud_keep_drop()`。这一条最容易写错

**成本。** 多一个线程栈。registrar 只走明文小请求（缓冲都在 PSRAM 不在栈上），8192 够，不必给 16384。会话线程栈从 88 KB 到 96 KB。中间队列多压 2–3 个 buffer ≈ 26–39 KB PSRAM（16 MB 池子，无所谓）。

**算术。** 1.90 → 2.29 项/s，**+20.5%**。

**风险。** 中。teardown 竞态是真实风险，`producers_done` / `abort` / `stop_capture` 三个标志的交互本来就已经不简单。

**判定：做，但排在①②之后**，而且要单独一次上板验证 teardown（尤其是会话中途按 BACK）。

### ④ `IMAGE_QUEUE_SLOTS` 2 → 4

**机制。** 2 个槽意味着两个 worker 一忙采样器立刻溢出。加深把"丢帧"变成"延迟"，而 `produced_ms` 现在正确携带，延迟上传不影响时间戳精度。

**改动面。** Kconfig 一个 default（range 已允许到 8）。`social_queue_flush()` 的栈数组按常量定尺，18 → 20 槽 × ~40 B = 800 B，16 KB 栈无压力。

**算术。** 不直接提高容量，是让采样器能在不丢帧的前提下压到真实容量。今天 3 次丢帧 / 106 帧；深度翻倍后自适应底线能探得更准。

**风险。** 低。唯一代价是情绪结果的年龄增加约 1 个 put 时间（~874 ms），在 `ALERT_WINDOW_MS=20000` 面前可忽略。

**判定：做。**

### ⑤ `AUDIO_CHUNK_MS` 2000 → 4000

**机制。** 音频占 164 项里的 61 项（37%），只贡献 22% 的字节。在一个"总项数有硬上限"的系统里，减少音频项数是直接换图片项数。

**改动面。** Kconfig 一个 default（range 500–5000 允许）。`SOCIAL_CHUNK_BYTES` = 16000×2×(4000/1000) = 128000 B PCM（每会话一次 PSRAM 分配，从 64 KB 涨到 128 KB，无所谓）；`SOCIAL_OGG_BYTES=32768` 对 4 s @24 kbps ≈ 12 KB 仍然够。

**算术。** 在 2.29 项/s 的容量下：
- 音频 2000 ms → 0.50 项/s，图片得 1.79/s（559 ms 间隔）
- 音频 4000 ms → 0.25 项/s，图片得 2.04/s（490 ms 间隔），**+14%**

在今天 1.90 的容量下是 1.40 → 1.65/s，**+18%**。

**风险。** 偏离文档的"2s 发送一次音频"，且云端 ASR 可能对分段长度有预期。**但 `audioTimeline` 已经连续 6 次会话为空**——这 37% 的上传工作目前产出为零。

**判定：需要你定。** 我倾向**先修音频为什么空，再决定这个**。拿一个已经坏掉的功能换吞吐，方向不对；等它能出转写了再谈块长，才知道 4 s 会不会伤到它。

## 明确否掉的方案

### ⑧ 预取 register 票据（msgId + presignedUrl 池）— **驳回**

上一轮我把它列为"收益最大但牺牲时间戳精度"。重新算过之后它是**被③严格支配的**：

预取后 transferrer 周期同样是 put = 874 ms，2 池位 → 同样 2.29 项/s。**和③一个数**，因为墙是池位不是 reg。所以它多付的时间戳误差（票据铸造时刻 vs 快门时刻）换来零收益。

这条也给出一个通用结论：**一旦 put 成为约束，所有只动 reg 的改动对吞吐都归零。**①②因此只值它们的延迟/抖动收益和极低的成本，不该被当成吞吐手段。

### ⑦ 提高 `CONN_POOL_SIZE` 和 `TLS_RAW_BUF_COUNT` — **RAM 不允许**

`CONFIG_MBEDTLS_SSL_IN_CONTENT_LEN=16384` 且 `OUT_CONTENT_LEN=16384`，每个活跃 SSL context 光记录缓冲就 ~33 KB，加 ctr_drbg / config ≈ **34 KB/连接**。

```
CONFIG_RAM_SIZE                    = 336 KB
会话线程栈 16+32+16+16+8           =  88 KB
当前 2 池位 × 34 KB + 2×8 KB 缓冲  =  84 KB
                                     ------
                                      172 KB (51%)  ← 还没算 IOB(60 buf)、LVGL
```

- 3 池位：+34+8 = +42 KB → 214 KB（64%），勉强
- 4 池位：+68+16 = +84 KB → 256 KB（**76%**），不可行

唯一出路是把 `OUT_CONTENT_LEN` 降到 4096（我们控制自己发什么，安全），per-connection 降到 ~21 KB。但 `IN_CONTENT_LEN` **不能降**——不带 MFL 扩展协商就降，对端发 16 KB 记录会直接断连，而很多服务器忽略 MFL。而且这是 board/ 的 defconfig，影响全系统所有 TLS 使用者（LLM、ASR、TTS）。

**判定：任何低风险形态下都不可执行。2.29 项/s 是这个设计的实际天花板。**

### ⑥ 干掉 10 ms 排空等待 — 做，但收益小

`poll(fd, POLLIN, 0)` 先探再读，几行，external/ 托管文件（需重算 manifest 摘要）。164 项 × 10 ms = 1.64 s/会话，占单项 0.95%。TTS 下载同样受益。零风险但也几乎零收益，值得搭在下次 external/ 改动里一起做，不值得单独动摘要。

int "VelaSight social image upload queue depth (frames)"
	default 4
	range 1 8
	depends on LVX_USE_DEMO_CONTEST2026_264_VELASIGHT
	---help---
		How many captured frames may wait for the uploader.  Full means
		the oldest is dropped and the sampler slows down.

		Shallow on purpose: an emotion result is about the moment it was
		sampled, so a queue that holds a long backlog spends the uplink on
		faces that have stopped being current.

		Two was too shallow, and the reason is the worker count rather
		than the depth itself.  With VS_SOCIAL_UPLOAD_WORKERS at 2, both
		slots are emptied the instant both workers are free and refilled
		while both are busy, so the queue is either empty or overflowing
		and the sampler is driven by whichever it hit last.  Measured
		2026-09-07 across two sessions: three drop events each, and the
		sampler spent most of both sessions in the slow half of its range
		walking back from them.

		Four decouples the two.  What it costs is frame age, and that cost
		is now bounded and paid honestly: an item carries the capture
		instant in vs_cloud_media_packet_s::produced_ms, so a frame that
		waited an extra slot is still reported to the cloud with the
		timestamp of the moment it was taken, not the moment it was sent.
		Before that field existed, deepening this queue would have skewed
		the emotion timeline; now it only delays a result.

		The bound: at the measured transfer rate a slot is about one
		second, so four slots is a worst-case age of a few seconds against
		a VS_SOCIAL_ALERT_WINDOW_MS of 20 s.  Do not raise it much further
		without revisiting that comparison -- the point of the queue is to
		absorb jitter, not to store a conversation.

		Overflow is not only absorbed here, it is fed back:
		CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_IMAGE_INTERVAL_MAX_MS describes how far the
		sampler backs off when this fills, and social_state_s's
		image_floor_ms remembers the rate that did it.

建议顺序 1 执行完毕，build20 构建干净。

## 四项改动

**① 明文请求合并成单次 send**（`vs_cloud.c` `cloud_plain_http_once()`）

register 原来是 ~300 B header 一次 `send()`、224 B body 再一次。第二次是个不满段，TCP 会扣着它等第一段的 ACK —— 请求还没到服务器就先赔一个 RTT。`hdr_cap` = `CLOUD_PATH_MAX + 512` ≈ 4 KB，body 最长 224 B，直接 memcpy 到 header 后面单次发出。

守卫是 `body_len <= hdr_cap - pos`，**回落路径不是死代码**：`VS_SOCIAL_CLOUD_TLS=n` 时预签名 PUT 也走这个函数，带着整张 JPEG，那种既不能拷也放不进去。

**② `TCP_NODELAY`**（`cloud_connect()`，加了 `#include <netinet/tcp.h>`）

和①不互相取代：①管一个请求内部，②管请求之间。这条 socket 上每次交换都是"发一个小请求然后等答复"，下一个请求依赖这次的响应所以还不存在，Nagle 要等的那个合并对象根本不会来。返回值故意忽略——不支持 `TCP_NODELAY` 的栈只是慢，不该因此拒绝连接。

**③ poll 给 register 让路**（新 `vs_cloud_cleartext_busy()` + `SOCIAL_POLL_YIELD_MAX 2`）

没有把标志穿过四层调用链，锁本身就是信号：trylock 成功就立刻解锁返回 false，失败说明有人正在交换。这是**探测不是预约**——答案可能过期，但对唯一的调用者无所谓：探漏了就照旧排队，探早了损失一个周期。

放在 `social_advice_sweep()` 和 `social_alert_release_stale()` **之后**，所以让掉的周期照样按时推进 alert 状态。上限 2 次是安全网：万一探测永远返回 true，最多饿 3 s（`ALERT_WINDOW_MS` 20 s、`ADVICE_TIMEOUT_MS` 30 s 都远大于此），之后照常阻塞拿锁。

**④ `IMAGE_QUEUE_SLOTS` 2 → 4**

2 个槽的问题不在深度而在 worker 数：两个 worker 同时空闲就把两个槽清空、同时繁忙就溢出，队列非空即满，采样器只能被上一次撞到的那头驱动。

Kconfig help 里记下了为什么现在加深是安全的：`produced_ms` 携带的是快门时刻，多等一个槽的帧仍然带着真实拍摄时间戳报给云端。**这个字段存在之前加深队列会歪掉情绪时间线，现在只是延迟一个结果。**

**⑤ 分类型 PUT 测量**（6 个计数器 + 第四行日志）

```
vs_social: transfer: image N x B B in M ms avg (X.X KB/s), audio N x B B in M ms avg (X.X KB/s)
```

整会话均值而不是 10 项窗口——一个窗口里两种类型都太少，平均不出东西。按 `payload_sent` 守卫，mock 云跳过的 PUT 不会被当成 0 ms 计入。

## 下次上板要读的三个数

1. **reg 最低窗口值**：build18 是 69/70/70，①应该把它压到 30–40（少一个 RTT）

另外 `image queue full, dropped` 应该明显减少甚至归零，采样器该稳在 500–750 ms 而不是在 1250–2000 之间来回走。

Looking at the build20 log from the first on-board run with the four step-1 changes. The session started mid-way through at 10:12:19 with the camera stopping at 10:14:16, and I'm examining the capture statistics showing about 185 frames captured over roughly two minutes with a measured frame rate of 1.51 fps, though there were some sampler skips on the hardware bus.

The realign counter is showing a nonsensical value again (9.97e16), which indicates that metric is still broken, and the core clock measurement is also unreliable as usual. However, the error counts remain clean with zero errors on both jpeg and yuv_buf, and the upstream rate band is still holding steady. Looking at the upload windows across the 16 captured intervals, I'm seeing fairly consistent performance with register and put operations distributed across each window, though there's some variability in the total bytes transferred per window ranging from around 600 to 1400 bytes. Finishing the calculation for the registration times, which averages out to about 181 milliseconds across all 18 windows.

Now I'm computing the same metrics for the put operation times, which sum to 15,300 milliseconds for an average of 850 ms. Comparing these results to the previous build session shows the item mean improved slightly by 1.3%, though the put operation appears to be taking considerably longer.

Looking at the registration times more closely, I notice something unexpected—the mean actually increased by 4.6% rather than improving as I'd hoped. Examining the distribution reveals the minimum got slightly better but the maximum spiked significantly higher, suggesting the changes introduced more variability rather than reducing it.

This is a critical finding: if coalescing the header and body truly eliminated a full round trip, the minimum should have dropped much further. Since it barely budged, either the 69 ms floor represents a single RTT plus server processing rather than two RTTs, or the coalesce optimization isn't actually being applied to the register body. I need to verify whether the body is actually taking that code path. The poll is now carrying more message IDs because the queue slots increased from 2 to 4, and I'm seeing higher inflight counts in the logs—averaging around 2.2 compared to 1.6 before. Bigger poll requests mean bigger responses, which extends the lock hold time and explains why the tail latency got worse instead of better.

But there's something more critical: the session actually aborted. The social stage timed out after 110 seconds on page 13, and the session was terminated before the logging could complete—that's why the advice line is missing from the tail.

Looking at the logs, the spoken-minutes download stalled after the first chunk and never resumed. The UI's per-stage deadline fired, the session aborted, and the partial WAV file left on the card is unplayable because the header couldn't be parsed—errno 61 indicates missing data.

This is a regression: the record R0000026 was already marked complete at 10:15:11, but then the TTS download stalled, leaving an inconsistency where the record claims completion but its WAV is truncated. Tracing the timeline, the first 131072-byte window finished in 2.4 seconds at about 53 KB/s, then the second window attempt appears to have failed.

The second Range request hung silently for 107 seconds until the UI's stage deadline fired, which suggests the TLS socket's read timeout (120 seconds) was blocking indefinitely while the UI gave up first. No error was logged—it just hung, which is the same `-0x004C MBEDTLS_ERR_NET_RECV_FAILED` socket timeout issue I identified earlier, except this time without any error message surfacing.

The real bug is that the retry logic (`CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS=4`) can never activate because the UI's 110-second stage deadline kills the session before the 120-second TLS read timeout can expire and trigger a proper transport error. The numbers check out: download started at 10:15:13.9, UI timeout fired at 10:17:01.25 (107.3 seconds), and the stage deadline of 110 seconds from 10:15:11.2 puts the cutoff at exactly 10:17:01.2.

Now I'm noticing something different in this session—the audio timeline finally has content with 3 samples, and the text fetch returned only 21 bytes instead of the previous 39, suggesting actual data came through this time rather than an error message.

The alert situation is unclear though. I see 2 extreme frames detected, which should trigger something given the 40 confidence threshold, but I don't see any alert raised or ignored messages in the logs. The capture window started mid-session around 10:12:19, so the relevant alert logic might have happened before the logging began.

What's more concerning is that `social_log_totals()` never executed because the session aborted. That means the emotion, advice, and transfer metrics I specifically built this for didn't get logged — the diagnostics are most valuable when things fail, yet the abort path skips them entirely. Now I need to trace through the drop and sampler behavior to understand what happened.

Looking at the timing, there were 3 drops total: 1 mid-session and 2 during finalization, which matches the pattern from build18. The image queue reached its full capacity of 4/4 before dropping, so the deeper queue is being used but still overflowing. The driver processed 185 frames while the app only consumed 133.

Calculating the total upload: 130 images (133 consumed minus 3 dropped) plus approximately 57 audio chunks gives around 187 items uploaded in 121.7 seconds, which is about 1.54 items per second. That's a 19% improvement over build18's 1.29 items per second. The image throughput alone was 1.07 items per second.

The real insight is that the capacity barely changed—both builds can theoretically handle around 1.9 items per second with 2 workers—but utilization jumped from 68% to 80%. The deeper queue is keeping the workers fed and busy, which is exactly what optimization ④ was supposed to do. So the win here came from queue depth, not from the registration or request improvements.

Looking at the detailed results: audio timeline finally has data (3 samples), the extreme frame detector caught both outliers through polling, and the driver metrics stay clean. But registration got worse—mean latency increased from 173 to 181 ms, and the max spiked to 396 ms. The Nagle hypothesis doesn't hold up; that ~65 ms floor appears to be one round trip plus cloud processing, not two. The tail latency degradation likely stems from increased inflight requests.

The session aborted after downloading only the first chunk of spoken minutes, then hit 107 seconds of silence before the UI deadline fired at 110 seconds. There's a timeout inversion bug: the socket timeout is set to 120 seconds but the UI stage deadline is 110 seconds, so the transport can never report a stalled read before the session gets killed—the retry logic becomes unreachable. The record was marked complete despite the download stalling partway through.

The abort path also skipped the diagnostics logging, so the transfer measurements and emotion/advice data never printed. The cycle counter and clock measurements are corrupted again. The actual wait time was about 51 seconds, well within budget, but the download stage itself is what terminated the session. I need to verify the timeout configuration and trace where the stage deadline is being set.

Looking at the numbers more carefully: the social stage timed out after 110 seconds, but the LLM socket timeout is 120 seconds—those are inverted. For the download stall, the first window showed 53 KB/s throughput, so the remaining 258 KB should have taken about 5 seconds, but it sat for 107 seconds and produced nothing, confirming it genuinely stalled rather than just running slow. Now I'm checking whether the polling mechanism is even triggering—it only yields when the cleartext busy flag returns true, so I need to trace that condition.

The real issue is I have no observability into whether the polling fired at all. The regression could mean either the polling didn't activate or it did but the larger uploads from the deeper queue overwhelmed any benefit. The higher inflight count makes sense if more images are being queued and uploaded, generating more message IDs per unit time, plus those two extreme frames that got held waiting for advice are also inflating the numbers.

Now I need to be honest about what happened: my prediction didn't pan out, and I should revise my model. The registration latency's 181 ms tail appears to be queuing behind larger poll responses, not what I initially expected. For the put operation at 850 ms mean, the minimum of 474 ms suggests an upload rate around 25.7 KB/s, which is roughly half the download speed—consistent with an asymmetric connection. Without the transfer timing breakdown I still can't fully decompose where the latency lives, so that measurement remains critical.

Now I'm checking the register values: `dma_remain` dropped from 1204 to 10240, and `last_status` changed from 0x00000001 to 0x00000002—both minor shifts. The frame and start-of-frame values are now perfectly aligned at 2160, which is cleaner than build18's slight mismatch. I'll lay out the numbers and the bug list with recommendations, keeping everything read-only since we're just documenting findings.

build20 首次上板。结果是**混合的**：吞吐确实涨了，但涨的原因不是我预测的那个，而①②基本失败。而且这次会话**中途 abort 了**，暴露出一个真实的超时倒置 bug。

## 我的预测错了

Here is the current code behind all four symptoms, in the order you asked.

## 1. The windowed download — `vs_cloud_download_to_file()`

Entry chain: `social_collect_minutes()` → `social_stage(VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_FETCHING)` (vs_social.c:3608) → `social_fetch_minutes_audio()` (vs_social.c:3416) → `vs_cloud_download_to_file(url, path, CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_MAX_BYTES, &file_len)` (vs_social.c:3437-3448) → **vs_cloud.c:4748**.

Knob defaults (vs_cloud.c:4582-4589), matching your config:

```c
#ifndef CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_WINDOW_BYTES
#  define CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_WINDOW_BYTES 131072
#endif
#ifndef CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS
#  define CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS 4
#endif
```

State set up before the loop (vs_cloud.c:4761-4766, 4781):

```c
size_t window = CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_WINDOW_BYTES;
unsigned int stalls = 0;
unsigned int requests = 0;
bool complete = false;
...
sink.next_report = CLOUD_DOWNLOAD_REPORT_STRIDE;   /* (128 * 1024), vs_cloud.c:4511 */
```

The attempt loop starts at **vs_cloud.c:4846** (`for (; ; )`) and is structured as: build a Range header, issue one blocking request, then classify the outcome.

```c
      if (window != 0)
        {
          snprintf(range, sizeof(range), "bytes=%zu-%zu", sink.written,
                   sink.written + window - 1);
          headers[0].name  = "Range";
          headers[0].value = range;
        }

      http = cloud_http_ex(parsed, "GET", window != 0 ? headers : NULL, NULL,
                           0, scratch, CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_REG_RESP_BYTES, NULL,
                           cloud_file_sink, &sink);
      got = sink.written - before;
      requests++;
```

Classification, in evaluation order:

- `sink.over || sink.err != 0` → break (budget exceeded or write() failed).
- `http < 0` (transport failure): if `window == 0` break; otherwise **every failure spends one attempt** — `if (++stalls >= CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS) break;` (vs_cloud.c:4906) — then prints and continues from `sink.written`, i.e. **resume, never restart**:
  ```c
  printf("%s: resuming %s from %zu bytes after %d (attempt %u of "
         "%d)\n", CLOUD_TAG, path, sink.written, http, stalls + 1,
         CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_DOWNLOAD_ATTEMPTS);
  ```
  A window that delivered bytes and then failed still consumes an attempt; only a *completed* response refills the budget (`stalls = 0;` on the 206 path, and on the Range-refused fallback).
- `http == 416` → `complete = sink.written != 0; break;` (object length was an exact multiple of the window).
- non-2xx → only one recovery: `window != 0 && sink.written == 0 && (http == 400 || http == 403 || http == 501)` prints `"%s refused a Range request (HTTP %d), retrying whole"`, sets `window = 0; stalls = 0;` and continues. Anything else breaks. This is the only "restart" in the function, and it can only fire before a single byte is stored.
- `window == 0 || http == 200` → whole-object response. If a window was already stored (`before != 0`) it refuses: prints `"answered a Range request with HTTP 200 at offset %zu, cannot resume"`, sets `http = -EPROTO`, breaks. Otherwise `complete = true`.
- otherwise 206 → `stalls = 0; if (got < window) { complete = true; break; }` — a short window is the last one, a full window means loop again.

**Deadlines: there are none in this function.** No wall clock is read anywhere in `vs_cloud_download_to_file()` — no per-window deadline, no overall deadline, no abort check. The only time bound on a request is the socket option: `CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_IO_TIMEOUT_MS` set as `SO_SNDTIMEO`/`SO_RCVTIMEO` (vs_cloud.c:1069-1071), plus the equivalent inside vela_tls per the header comment at vs_cloud.c:4562-4565. That means a request that keeps dribbling bytes (each read resetting the receive timer) never returns an error, `stalls` is never incremented, and the loop cannot notice. That is exactly the shape of your log: the second window's request went out at 10:15:13.915 and the function was still inside `cloud_http_ex()` 107 s later when the UI timer fired. The attempt budget only bounds *failed* requests, not a hung one.

The progress line comes from the sink, not the loop — `cloud_file_sink()` (vs_cloud.c ≈4735-4745):

```c
  sink->written += len;

  if (sink->written >= sink->next_report)
    {
      printf("%s: download %zu bytes\n", CLOUD_TAG, sink->written);
      sink->next_report = sink->written + CLOUD_DOWNLOAD_REPORT_STRIDE;
    }
```

`CLOUD_DOWNLOAD_REPORT_STRIDE` is 128 KiB = 131072, the same value as the window, so exactly one line prints per completed window and the first threshold coincides with the end of window 1. Your single `download 131072 bytes` line is "window 1 finished"; there is no per-window start/end log at all, which is why the second window is invisible.

Complete set of lines this path can emit: `"no %d byte download buffer, writing unaggregated"`, `"cannot download %s, unsupported scheme"`, `"cannot create %s: %d"`, `"download %zu bytes"`, `"resuming %s from %zu bytes after %d (attempt %u of %d)"`, `"%s refused a Range request (HTTP %d), retrying whole"`, `"%s answered a Range request with HTTP 200 at offset %zu, cannot resume"`, `"writing the last block of %s failed: %d"`, `"download exceeds the %zu byte budget"`, `"writing %s failed: %d"`, `"download of %s failed after %zu bytes: %d"`, `"download returned HTTP %d after %zu bytes"`, and on success only:

```c
printf("%s: %s written in %u write(s) of up to %zu bytes, %u request(s)\n",
       CLOUD_TAG, path, sink.writes,
       sink.cap != 0 ? sink.cap : sink.written, requests);   /* vs_cloud.c:5069 */
```

Every failure exit goes through `unlink_out:` and `unlink(path)`, so a failed download leaves no file. The tail flush only happens when `complete && !sink.over && sink.err == 0`.

The expression is two macros (vs_app.c:89-99):

```c
#ifndef CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS
#  define CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS 90000
#endif
...
#define VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS \
  (CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS + 20000)
```

`CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` is `default 90000, range 10000 300000` (Kconfig:1139-1143), so 90000 + 20000 = **110000**, which is the number in your log. Kconfig:1148-1152 states explicitly it is "Not enforced by the download itself".

Budgets are chosen per stage in `vs_social_stage_budget_ms()` (vs_app.c:1569-1602):

```c
  if (runtime->page != VS_PAGE_SOCIAL_FINALIZING)
    {
      return VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS;          /* 40000, vs_app.c:61 */
    }
  switch (runtime->social_stage)
    {
      case VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_WAITING:
        return VS_SOCIAL_FINALIZE_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS;  /* 60000 + 20000 = 80000 */
      case VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_FETCHING:
        return VS_SOCIAL_FETCH_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS;     /* 110000 */
      default:
        return VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS;           /* 40000 */
    }
```

So yes, stages get different budgets: FETCHING 110 s, WAITING 80 s, and NONE/STOPPING/CLOSING/SAVING plus every non-finalizing waiting page 40 s.

`page 13 stage 5`: stage 5 is `VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_FETCHING` — the enum in include/vs_app.h:64-74 is NONE=0, STOPPING=1, CLOSING=2, WAITING=3, SAVING=4, FETCHING=5, COUNT=6, which lines up with the six-entry `stalled[]` table in vs_app.c:1652-1661 whose sixth string is `"接收语音无响应"`. Page 13 is `VS_PAGE_SOCIAL_FINALIZING` (include/vs_types.h ≈166) — structurally it has to be, since FETCHING is only reachable under that page.

Arming and firing live in the main loop (vs_app.c ≈3130-3157):

```c
        bool waiting = vs_social_stage_is_waiting(runtime.page);
        if (!waiting)
          { runtime.social_stage_until_ms = 0; }
        else if (runtime.social_stage_until_ms == 0)
          { runtime.social_stage_until_ms =
              vs_app_now_ms() + vs_social_stage_budget_ms(&runtime); }
        else if ((int32_t)(runtime.social_stage_until_ms - vs_app_now_ms()) <= 0)
          {
            printf("velasight: social stage timed out on page %d stage %d "
                   "after %lu ms\n", (int)runtime.page,
                   (int)runtime.social_stage,
                   (unsigned long)vs_social_stage_budget_ms(&runtime));
            vs_social_stage_timeout(&runtime);
            vs_render(display, &runtime);
          }
```

The deadline is re-armed per stage (the `VS_APP_EVENT_SOCIAL_STAGE` handler at vs_app.c:2049-2062 updates `social_stage`, and the comment at 1576-1581 says each step refreshes this when it starts). Your timing confirms it: FETCHING was entered at ~10:15:11.2 and the timer fired at 10:17:01.25, 110 s later to the tenth.

What fires (vs_app.c:1646-1680, the `VS_PAGE_SOCIAL_FINALIZING` case of `vs_social_stage_timeout()`):

```c
          enum vs_social_stage_e stage = runtime->social_stage;

          vs_social_abort();
          vs_cancel_request(runtime);
          vs_set_error_reason(runtime, -ETIMEDOUT, vs_browse_page(runtime),
                              vs_social_can_retry(),
```

That `vs_social_abort()` is what printed `vs_social: aborted`. Note `vs_social_can_retry()` is still true at this point, because `retry_ready` is only cleared *after* the fetch returns (vs_social.c:3618-3620), so the error page offered a retry.

## 3. Record write ordering — `social_persist_minutes()`

The finalize tail is `social_collect_minutes()` (vs_social.c:3495). Order is: WAITING poll loop (3525-3562, bounded by `CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_FINALIZE_TIMEOUT_MS`) → minutes summary log → **SAVING → record written** → **FETCHING → audio downloaded**:

```c
  social_stage(VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_SAVING);                    /* 3589 */
  ret = social_persist_minutes(&minutes, body, record_key,
                               sizeof(record_key));        /* 3590 */
  ...
  social_stage(VS_SOCIAL_STAGE_FETCHING);                  /* 3608 */
  (void)social_fetch_minutes_audio(minutes.tts_url, record_key, audio,
                                   sizeof(audio));         /* 3609 */
```

So the record is committed to SD-NAND **before** the spoken minutes are fetched, and the fetch result is explicitly discarded (`(void)`, with the comment at 3601-3607 saying a failure here does not fail the session).

`incomplete` is set only from the text/timeline, never from audio (vs_social.c:3330-3332):

```c
  index.incomplete = minutes->summary[0] == '\0' ||
                     minutes->emotion_samples == 0;
```

In your session the cloud gave a summary and emotion samples, so `incomplete = false` — that is why the log reads `record R0000026 saved (complete, calm 93 happy 0 tense 7)` (printf at vs_social.c ≈3341-3344). "complete" here means "the cloud answered", not "the audio is on the card".

There is **no rewrite path**. `struct vs_history_index_s` (include/vs_history.h:29-41) has no tts/audio member at all — `kind, record_key, date, title, summary, calm, happy, tense, incomplete` — and the public API is open/ready/count/get_index/snapshot/open_full/read_full/**append**/audio_path/close (include/vs_history.h:48-131). `vs_history_append()` is the only writer; nothing can amend or re-mark a record once written, so a record cannot be downgraded to "no audio" after a failed fetch.

The audio path is implicit, derived from the record key's sequence number (vs_history.c:74 and 296-301):

```c
#define VS_HISTORY_AUDIO_FMT  "%s/R%07u.WAV"
...
  snprintf(path, path_len, VS_HISTORY_AUDIO_FMT, g_history_dir[kind], seq);
```

Both the writer (`social_fetch_minutes_audio()`, vs_social.c:3437) and the reader (`vs_update_record_audio()`, vs_app.c:1713-1740) call `vs_history_audio_path()` and get `/mnt/sdnand/ai_agent/history/social/R0000026.WAV` with no existence or validity check. Playback then reports whatever `vs_tts_wav_open()` returns (vs_tts.c:479-491):

```c
      printf("%s: %s %s (%d)\n", VS_TTS_TAG, path,
             ret == -ENOENT ? "has no audio" : "is unplayable", ret);
```

Your `-61` took the "is unplayable" branch, i.e. the open got past "file missing" and the header/data check rejected it. I did not read `vs_tts_wav_open()`, so I can't say which specific check produced -61.

## 4. The abort unwind

`vs_social_abort()` (vs_social.c:4325-4371), called from the UI thread:

```c
  vs_tts_stop();                       /* outside the lock, before the check */
  pthread_mutex_lock(&g_social.lock);
  if (!g_social.running)
    { pthread_mutex_unlock(&g_social.lock); return; }   /* silent early out */
  g_social.abort        = true;
  g_social.stop_capture = true;
  g_social.paused       = false;
  pthread_cond_broadcast(&g_social.cond);
  vs_media_stream_wake(g_social.camera, true);
  vs_audio_capture_abort(g_social.mic);
  pthread_mutex_unlock(&g_social.lock);

  printf("%s: aborted\n", SOCIAL_TAG);   /* vs_social.c:4369 */
```

So `vs_social: aborted` is printed **by the UI thread, from `vs_social_abort()` itself** — it reports that the flag was set, not that the worker observed it. Nothing here interrupts a socket read.

Where the flag is observed: only in the WAITING poll loop (vs_social.c:3541-3551), which returns early with `"finalize abandoned while %s"`, and in the session worker's own sampling loop (vs_social.c:3905-3924). There is **no abort check in the FETCHING step and none inside the download**, so at abort time the worker was blocked in `cloud_http_ex()` and stayed there.

Reachability of `social_log_totals()`:

```c
  if (aborting)
    { goto stop; }                 /* vs_social.c:3921-3924 */
  ...
  social_finalize_sequence();      /* 3940 */
  social_log_totals();             /* 3941 */
  social_release_devices();        /* 3942 */
  goto done;

stop:
  social_stop_producers();         /* 3946 */
  social_log_totals();             /* 3947 */

release:
  social_queue_flush();
  social_release_devices();

close_session:
  ... vs_cloud_social_finalize(...) /* close abandoned session */
```

Both exits call it, so the totals are structurally reachable on the abort path too — but only for an abort seen by the sampling loop (case `stop:`). For an abort during finalize, the worker is already past that loop; `social_collect_minutes()` returning (early-abandon, `social_fail_finalize()`, or success) unwinds through `social_finalize_sequence()` back to line 3940 and *then* prints the totals. That is why your log has no totals: the thread never returned from `vs_cloud_download_to_file()`, so line 3941 was never reached. The totals were not skipped by the abort path; they were parked behind the deadline-less download.

The normal path differs only in ordering and in what precedes it: `social_finalize_sequence()` joins the producers via `social_stop_producers()` on the way in (so the counters are final and the tail audio chunk is included), then totals, then `social_release_devices()` — versus `stop:` which stops producers, prints totals, flushes the queue, releases devices, and then closes the abandoned cloud session so the next attempt doesn't hit -EBUSY. Also note that after an abort the worker still runs the rest of `social_collect_minutes()` when the download eventually returns: it posts `SOCIAL_RESULT` (dropped by the UI, since the handler at vs_app.c:2065 requires `page == VS_PAGE_SOCIAL_FINALIZING`), acks, and can call `vs_tts_play(audio)` — after `vs_tts_stop()` already ran — before printing `"finalize complete in %lu ms"`.

## Extra: the poll-yield block and neighbouring counters

The block is in `social_poll_once()`, vs_social.c ≈2603-2638, immediately after the scratch NULL check and before the inflight snapshot:

```c
  {
    static unsigned int yielded;

    if (yielded < SOCIAL_POLL_YIELD_MAX && vs_cloud_cleartext_busy())
      {
        yielded++;
        return;
      }

    yielded = 0;
  }
```

`SOCIAL_POLL_YIELD_MAX` is 2 (vs_social.c:158). `vs_cloud_cleartext_busy()` is the `pthread_mutex_trylock(&g_cloud_keep_lock)` probe at vs_cloud.c:400-410 (declared include/vs_cloud.h:607). The count is a function-static on purpose — the comment at 2622-2626 notes only the session thread runs this, so it needs neither the lock nor a home in `g_social`, and it is deliberately *not* reset between sessions.

If a per-session yield count were wanted, `struct social_state_s` (vs_social.c ≈405-690) already holds these counter groups, all printed by `social_log_totals()` (vs_social.c:3176-3272) and reset in the state clear at vs_social.c ≈4141-4146:

- transport: `image_seq`, `audio_seq`, `dropped_image`, `dropped_audio`, `uploaded`, `upload_failed` (≈448-455)
- coalescing bookkeeping: `drop_reported`, `drop_report_ms`, `upload_reported`, `upload_window_ms` (≈541-544), `upload_register_ms`, `upload_transfer_ms` (≈555-556)
- per-type transfer: `upload_image_put_ms`, `upload_audio_put_ms`, `upload_image_bytes`, `upload_audio_bytes`, `upload_image_count`, `upload_audio_count` (≈581-586)
- `inflight_evicted` (≈605) — the closest analogue, a "the device gave up on something" count
- emotion: `emotion_results`, `emotion_extreme`, `emotion_low_conf`, `results_repeated`, `failed_results`, `alerts_raised` (≈665-670)
- advice: `advice_delivered`, `advice_discarded`, `advice_refused`, `advice_expired` (just below the emotion block)

The emotion/advice group and `inflight_evicted` are the natural neighbours: same lock, same reset, and `social_log_totals()` already prints them from both worker exits (3941 and 3947).

  1. app/velasight/vs_cloud.c — Holds vs_cloud_download_to_file() (4748) with the Range attempt loop (4846), the attempt accounting (4906), the "download %zu bytes" sink report, the final "written in N write(s) ... N request(s)" line (5069), and the absence of any deadline — the direct cause of the 107 s silence
  2. app/velasight/vs_social.c — social_persist_minutes() (3291) and the SAVING-before-FETCHING order in social_collect_minutes() (3589-3609), vs_social_abort() and its "aborted" print (4369), the worker's abort vs finalize exits around social_log_totals() (3921-3947), and the SOCIAL_POLL_YIELD_MAX block (2629) plus the social_state_s counters

  /* Alert debounce.  See the file header for what alert_gen is for. */

  uint32_t alert_gen;

  /* When the last SOCIAL_ALERT_NEEDED extreme frames arrived, as a ring.
   *
   * This replaced a plain consecutive counter, and the reason is arithmetic.
   * The counter required N extreme results in a row and was reset by any
   * result that was not extreme -- but the stream it counts is neither dense
   * nor clean.  Measured 2026-09-07: 43 images uploaded produced 7 emotion

   *
   * A window asks the question that was meant instead: were there N extreme
   * readings within CONFIG_VS_SOCIAL_ALERT_WINDOW_MS.  A calm reading no longer
   * erases the evidence, it just stops adding to it, and the window expiring is
   * what forgets.
   */

  uint64_t extreme_at[SOCIAL_ALERT_STAMP_MAX];
  uint8_t  extreme_head;
  uint8_t  extreme_have;
  uint8_t  calm_streak;
  bool     alert_active;

   * Cleared on every raise, because it is a property of one alert.
   *
   * This is what bounds the wait described on social_awaiting_advice().  That
   * wait is right while the advice is still coming and wrong once it has
   * arrived, and the difference matters because the two timers disagree by a
   * lot: an alert is meant to release VS_SOCIAL_ALERT_HOLD_MS (12 s) after the
   * last extreme frame, but an entry keeps waiting for
   * VS_SOCIAL_ADVICE_TIMEOUT_MS (30 s), and the cloud advises once per extreme
   * run rather than once per red frame -- so most of those waits are for advice
   * that was never coming.
   *
   * Replaying the 2026-09-07 19:55 session against the fixed confidence floor,
   * the last red frame was at 19:55:57 and the five entries behind it swept out
   * one by one until 19:56:28.  The alert would have sat on screen for 31 s
   * after the conversation calmed, holding for advice it had already been
   * given at 19:55:44.
   */

  bool     alert_advised;
  uint64_t alert_since_ms;

  /* What the cloud actually answered, counted so a session can be read as a
   * whole rather than reconstructed from the per-occurrence lines.
   *
   * These exist because the previous session could not be accounted for from
   * its log.  It showed about fifty extreme readings and ended with a summary
   * claiming the conversation was 97% calm, and there was no way to tell
   * whether the device had seen fifty frames or the same few frames fifty
   * times.  results_repeated answers exactly that; failed_results is the
   * "no usable face" count the cloud's own yield question needs, which its
   * status 30 otherwise hides.
   */

  uint32_t emotion_results;   /* msgEvent 0 results folded in, once each */
  uint32_t emotion_extreme;   /* of those, red */
  uint32_t emotion_low_conf;  /* red, but under the confidence floor */
  uint32_t results_repeated;  /* results the cloud re-sent, ignored here */
  uint32_t failed_results;    /* peer status 30, whatever its real reason */
  uint32_t alerts_raised;

   * advice sent by the cloud and thrown away here, plus six frames the cloud

   * last frame of it, not once per red frame.  Read as six cloud failures it
   * pointed at the wrong side entirely; discarded is the number to act on.

  uint32_t advice_delivered;  /* reached the screen */
  uint32_t advice_discarded;  /* arrived, but no alert it still described */
  uint32_t advice_refused;    /* status 30 on the wait: cloud says never */
